market_context: United States/Canada; household troubleshooting for a toilet tank that keeps filling or leaks into the bowl through the flush seal, chain, float, fill valve or overflow tube.
title: Why Does My Toilet Keep Running? Common Causes and Fixes

seo.title: Toilet Keeps Running: Common Causes and Fixes
seo.meta_description: Check the flush seal, chain, water level, float and fill valve. Learn to separate a leak into the bowl from a fill valve that never shuts off.
seo.search_intent: Diagnose why a toilet tank keeps running after a flush and correct the most common household causes without replacing parts at random.

excerpt: If your toilet keeps running after the tank fills, look inside the tank. If water is leaking into the bowl, the flush seal may not be closing or the chain may be holding it open. If water rises into the overflow tube, check the float and fill valve. A simple food-coloring test can confirm a quiet tank-to-bowl leak.
content_html:
A toilet that keeps making noise after a flush can waste water in two different ways. In one, the tank reaches its normal level but water slowly leaks into the bowl, causing the fill valve to cycle back on. In the other, incoming water never shuts off and the level rises into the overflow tube.

Separating those behaviors prevents unnecessary parts replacement: first see where the water is going, then inspect the component that controls that path.

Remove the tank lid and watch one complete cycle

Set the lid somewhere safe and flush. Watch the flush mechanism open, close and refill.

Identify the flush seal or flapper, chain or button linkage, vertical overflow tube and the fill valve with its float. Modern tanks may use a canister instead of a traditional flapper, but the basic logic is similar.

If water is leaking into the bowl, suspect the seal first

The flush seal should close tightly after the flush. If it is warped, hardened, coated with mineral deposits or not seated correctly, a quiet stream can continue into the bowl.

Kohler recommends checking whether gently pressing the flapper or canister seal into place stops the running. If it does, you have found a likely cause.

The chain can be too short or too long

A chain that is too tight can hold the seal slightly open. One with excessive slack can get caught under the flapper or tangle with other tank parts.

There should be some slack when the mechanism is closed, but not enough to snag. Make a small adjustment and test several flushes.

A food-coloring test can confirm a silent leak

If the toilet seems quiet but you suspect water loss, add a few drops of food coloring to the tank without flushing. Wait about 10–15 minutes.

If colored water appears in the bowl, water is crossing the flush valve. That points the diagnosis toward the seal, seat or related mechanism rather than the fill valve.

If water reaches the overflow tube, look at the float

The fill valve should shut off before water reaches the top of the overflow tube. If the float is adjusted too high, the tank keeps filling and the excess runs down the overflow into the bowl.

Adjust the water level according to the tank markings or manufacturer instructions. Kohler gives roughly one inch below the top of the overflow tube as a general reference for certain designs, but your toilet may have a specific fill line.

If the float rises but water keeps entering

That points more directly to the fill valve. Sediment, wear or an internal failure can prevent it from shutting off even after the float reaches its normal position.

Some fill valves have a manufacturer-approved cleaning procedure; on others, replacing the compatible valve is more practical than taking it apart blindly.

Check the small refill tube

The narrow tube from the fill valve directs water into the overflow tube during refill so the bowl reaches the correct level. If it is misplaced or pushed too deeply into the overflow, some designs can refill incorrectly or siphon.

Position it exactly as the manufacturer specifies, typically clipped above the water level and aimed into the overflow rather than sealed deeply inside it.

Mineral buildup can interfere with sealing

Hard-water deposits can accumulate around the flush-valve seat and moving components. Where the manufacturer allows cleaning, remove deposits with a method compatible with rubber, plastic and porcelain.

Avoid aggressive metal scraping on sealing surfaces because a scratch can create a permanent leak.

Before replacing parts, shut off water and identify the model

If you plan to remove a seal or valve, locate the toilet shutoff first and make sure it works. Empty the tank according to the repair procedure.

Parts are not universally interchangeable. Identify or measure the flush mechanism and buy a component designed for the toilet.

When the problem is no longer just inside the tank

If water is on the floor, moisture appears around the base, the tank is cracked, the shutoff valve leaks or supply connections drip, stop treating it as a simple running-toilet problem. Those are plumbing leaks that can damage materials.

Call a plumber if the shutoff will not close, parts are broken or unclear, or the tank continues to leak after the confirmed component has been correctly replaced.

The fastest diagnostic sequence

Watch the water level. If it stays below the overflow but dye moves into the bowl, focus on the flush seal and chain. If water runs into the overflow, focus on water level, float and fill valve.

A running toilet is usually showing you where the water is escaping. Watching one full cycle is often more useful than buying parts first.

faq.question: Why does my toilet refill every few minutes when nobody uses it?
faq.answer: A slow tank-to-bowl leak through the flush seal often lowers the tank level enough to make the fill valve cycle on periodically.

faq.question: How can I tell whether the flapper is leaking?
faq.answer: Put food coloring in the tank without flushing. If color appears in the bowl, water is leaking through the flush mechanism.

faq.question: Why is water constantly going into the overflow tube?
faq.answer: The water level may be set too high or the fill valve may not be shutting off when the float rises.

faq.question: Do I need to replace the whole toilet?
faq.answer: Usually not. Many running-toilet problems are solved by adjusting or replacing a compatible flush seal, chain or fill valve.
